transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-11
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~50 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Lina Gomez (Redwood), Sophie Lang (RiverMark Head of ML), Daniel Kim (Infra Lead), Priya Shah (SecOps), Ethan Park (Product)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check, can everyone hear ok?
[00:04] Sophie Lang: Yep, hearing you, thanks Maya.
[00:07] Daniel Kim: Good here.
[00:10] Maya Chen: Awesome. Agenda for today: quick recap of last week's TTFT and streaming numbers, dig into sequence length distributions you shared, Arjun will walk through kernel selection impacts, then we align on next steps.
[00:22] Arjun Patel: Cool, I'll start with the numbers we ran yesterday. We re-ran the originial streaming test with prefix caching enabled and compared TTFT — time to first token — across three kernels: optimized-attn-v1, fused-attn-k, and the fallback generic kernel. Results: median TTFT improved about 18% on optimized-attn-v1 when streaming with small chunk size, but the p99 still spikes on longer sequences.
[00:45] Sophie Lang: Is that with kv cache warm or cold?
[00:49] Arjun Patel: Cold start for the run, but we also did warm cache runs. With warm K V cache the TTFT delta shrunk to ~8% since most overhead is in initial attention kernel setup. Also batching behavior changed — continuous batching helps throughput but can hurt TTFT for single-request low-latency flows.
[01:12] Priya Shah: Quick sec, can you remind me how streaming mode affects audit logs? We're concerned about partial responses and log completeness.
[01:20] Lina Gomez: Streaming doesn't change what we log, it just changes how tokens are emitted. You still get request/response trace ids, and we can ensure finalization events are logged once stream completes. We'll confirm exact retention with SecOps.
[01:33] Sophie Lang: Thanks. Back to TTFT, we saw on our side median ~120ms and p95 ~420ms on hosted baseline for seq_len about 512. Does that align?
[01:42] Arjun Patel: Yes, broadly. Our hosted baseline test on our curated 7B open model with quantization Q4 showed median ~110-130ms for seq_len 512, p95 around 380-450ms depending on kernel. For sequence length 1024 we see median move to ~170-220ms and p95 to ~700-900ms.
[02:05] Daniel Kim: For RiverMark the big concern is cold-start TTFT under bursty traffic — we have a p95 requirement under 500ms for interactive flows.
[02:13] Maya Chen: Right, so tradeoffs. For strict p95 SLOs we recommended dedicated capacity with warm pool and pre-warms. That keeps KV cache hot and gives predictable kernel placement. Hosted can meet median goals but p95 under bursts is trickier without reserved nodes.
[02:32] Ethan Park: Do we have numbers on pre-warm cost? We need to justify to finance.
[02:36] Arjun Patel: We'll put line-items in the spreadsheet. Rough back-of-envelope: holding a small warm pool for your traffic shape (from the sample you sent) increases cost about 12-15% vs bursty stateless, but it drops p95 by ~30-40%. We'll capture exact in bench sheet.
[02:56] Sophie Lang: On kernel choices — what's the difference between fused-attn-k and optimized-attn-v1 in terms of memory? Could we run fused on longer sequences?
[03:05] Arjun Patel: Fused-attn-k uses a different kernel path that's memory-optimized for medium lengths; optimized-attn-v1 is latency-optimized for short to medium. For long sequences (2k+) a generic kernel sometimes beats them because of tiling efficiency. It depends on model and quantization.
[03:26] Priya Shah: Are we talking about quantization causing different kernel picks? We plan to use INT8 for cost reasons.
[03:33] Arjun Patel: Yes. INT8 paths change SIMD usage and that can push the runtime to prefer different kernels. Our runtime has a kernel selector that uses model arch, seq_len histogram, and quant type to pick at runtime. We'll show the selector output in the profile.
[03:48] Daniel Kim: Can you show logs of kernel selection?
[03:51] Arjun Patel: Sure, later in the call I'll share a sample profile; we also can provide a profile file you can upload.
[03:59] Maya Chen: Sophie, you had sent a sequence length distribution earlier — looks like 60% under 512, 30% 512-1024, 10% 1024+. Is that still accurate?
[04:09] Sophie Lang: Yes, that's the 30k request sample from last week. Might shift during peak hours though.
[04:15] Arjun Patel: Ok good. That distribution explains why fused-attn-k gave slightly better throughput but optimized-attn-v1 had lower median TTFT on short collo flows.
[04:28] [05:00] Arjun Patel: We also tested streaming chunk sizes. Smaller chunk size (16 tokens) reduces TTFT marginally but increases compute overhead overall; larger chunk size (64) slightly increases TTFT but improves end-to-end throughput. For interactive UX, 32 token chunks seem like the best sweet spot for your traffic.
[05:25] Sophie Lang: On streaming, does Redwood support early partial responses for multi-tool pipelines? We have a tool orchestration that wants partials.
[05:33] Lina Gomez: Yes, we support tool-calling and structured partial emissions; we can include delimiter events so your orchestrator knows when a partial is final enough.
[05:40] Daniel Kim: Any impact on security or data residency with streaming?
[05:43] Maya Chen: No change to residency. Data stays in the region. For Private deployments we can ensure everything stays in your VPC and on-prem if needed.
[05:52] Priya Shah: Speaking of Private, you mentioned a private deployment earlier — timeline and complexity?
[05:57] Maya Chen: Private (VPC) has a longer lead time, typically 6-10 weeks for enterprise onboarding with KMS/HSM integrations and custom audit log pipelines. Dedicated reserved capacity is faster — 2-4 weeks to provision and pre-warm.
[06:12] Sophie Lang: We likely need VPC for compliance eventually, but for the POC dedicated sounds fine.
[06:18] Ethan Park: Any implications for SSO/SSO provisioning?
[06:21] Maya Chen: We support SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning and role-based RBAC in both Dedicated and Private. We'll share the security doc pack.
[06:29] Priya Shah: And SOC2?
[06:31] Lina Gomez: Redwood is SOC2 Type II compliant; we'll share the report via secure link.
[06:36] Arjun Patel: Back to tuning: aside from kernel selection we recommend three levers to hit your p95: 1) warm pool with pre-warmed KV caches, 2) streaming chunk size 32 + small prefix caching for typical prompts, 3) selective quantization profile for latency-sensitive routes (e.g., keep critical route at higher precision).
[06:56] Daniel Kim: About selective quantization — can we route some requests to a higher precision model for better tail latency?
[07:01] Arjun Patel: Yes, smart routing can send requests based on cost center, route, or latency budgets. We can set fallbacks so if the dedicated pool is saturated it routes to a cheaper hosted variant.
[07:11] Sophie Lang: Will the routing affect tokens cost reporting? We need per-route cost breakdown for product owners.
[07:16] Lina Gomez: We expose token-level cost in the Console and can give per-route dashboards.
[07:20] [07:30] Maya Chen: Ok, Arjun can you walk through the kernel profiling plan and what we need from RiverMark?
[07:35] Arjun Patel: Plan: 1) SE will run kernel selector with actual model binary and quant profile for seq_len buckets (256, 512, 1024, 2048). 2) We'll collect TTFT, median, p95, p99, and kernel choices for each bucket. 3) We'll re-run with streaming chunk sizes 16/32/64 and with KV cache warm vs cold. 4) We'll capture per-token compute and memory graphs. For inputs we need the model artifact or compatible repo, quantization settings, and a representative traffic sample (anonymized).
[08:10] Daniel Kim: We can share anonymized traces and an S3 link for the sample. Also we'll give the model artifact access via the secured bucket.
[08:18] Arjun Patel: Perfect. Also, to debug the p99 spikes we may want a short live run against a staging endpoint with traffic replay to capture cold-start behavior.
[08:27] Sophie Lang: We can do traffic replay in staging this week. Good.
[08:31] Priya Shah: For auditability, the logs from profiling — are they safe to share with third-party auditors?
[08:36] Lina Gomez: We'll scrub any customer-sensitive identifiers; the profiler outputs are meant for ops debugging. We'll also sign an NDA for any sensitive artifacts if needed.
[08:46] Ethan Park: Cost question again: if we do dedicated with 3 pre-warmed nodes is there autoscaling for sudden spikes?
[08:53] Arjun Patel: Yes, dedicated pools can have burst capacity and autoscale policies. There's a tradeoff: fast autoscale helps but cold starts happen. We recommend a small warm headroom plus burst autoscale with a fallback model for when saturation happens.
[09:06] Sophie Lang: Anything else on kernel choices?
[09:09] Arjun Patel: One more thing — compiler flags. We found that enabling layer-fused kernels and some math-library tuning improved TTFT for your model by about 7-9% but increased memory. We'll include those flags in the bench sheet and mark them as optional.
[09:25] [09:40] Maya Chen: Let's capture action items. Maya to send updated spreadsheet with cost lines and the tunings we discussed. Arjun to run kernel profiling on 256/512/1024/2048 seq_len buckets and streaming 16/32/64 chunks; include selector logs and kernel choices. RiverMark to share anonymized traffic sample, model artifact access, and SLOs. Priya to confirm KMS and log retention.
[09:58] Daniel Kim: One quick item — do you have recommendations on inference library versions? We're on an older CUDA stack for some nodes.
[10:04] Arjun Patel: We'll include minimum supported CUDA/CUDNN and a recommended stack in the bench doc; if your stack is older we'll note compatibility and expected perf delta.
[10:12] Priya Shah: Also, what about encryption at rest for logs?
[10:15] Lina Gomez: We support customer-managed keys in Dedicated and Private for logs and model storage; we'll include architecture diagram in the security pack.
[10:23] Sophie Lang: Sounds good. When's the follow-up?
[10:25] Maya Chen: Same time next week, 2027-05-18, unless something else pops up.
[10:29] Sophie Lang: Works for me.
[10:31] Maya Chen: Great — thanks everyone. We'll send notes and next steps after the call.

Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcription had some misrecognized acronyms ("K V cache" shown instead of KV cache, occasional speaker attribution mismatch), original recording available on request.

References shared: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/river_mark_latency_spreadsheet (Redwood internal bench sheet link placeholder), Security pack link: https://redwood.ai/security/soc2-report (placeholder).
